subsection: 4. Everyday expressions of culture and identity

notes.b: Culture and identity are the broad concepts. Everyday expressions are the visible parts of culture that people practise, and they are what an essay on this topic is built from.
points: Culture is a group's shared, learned way of life: its beliefs, customs, language, arts, food and dress. It is learned, not inherited, so each generation has to be taught it.
Identity is a person's or group's sense of who they are and where they belong, for example as Irish, Catalan or a member of a county club.
Everyday expressions are the visible, practised parts of culture: people choose them, repeat them and pass them on.
The main everyday expressions in this option are sport, traditions, costume, food, music, art and festivals.
notes.tip: Exams ask how people express their culture and identity in everyday life. Plan around sport, music and dance, festivals and traditions, food and costume, and art, with Irish and European examples.

notes.b: Customs are not just pastimes. They do real work for a group, and these five functions give you the points to explain in an essay.
points: They mark belonging: taking part in a shared custom shows that a person belongs to the group.
They pass culture from one generation to the next, because children learn the games, songs and customs by taking part.
They assert identity when a culture is under pressure, as Irish games and music did during the Gaelic Revival (a movement to bring Irish games and music back into everyday use).
They attract tourists and bring income to the places where they are practised.
They can also mark division: parades in Northern Ireland and football rivalries separate groups as well as unite them.
notes.tip: Don't give figures for visitor numbers or the economic value of festivals. Explain the function instead and name the example.

notes.h: Pressures on everyday culture: globalisation and Americanisation
notes.b: Globalisation (the growing connection between countries through trade, media and travel) spreads the same products, sports and customs to many countries, so cultures can become more alike.
points: Fast food, Hollywood films, global sports and global brands are the main channels of Americanisation (the spread of American culture to other countries).
McDonald's opened its first Irish restaurant on Grafton Street, Dublin, in 1977, an example of a global brand entering everyday Irish life.
Halloween customs returned from the USA in a commercial form, although the festival itself has Irish origins in Samhain (the Celtic festival of 31 October to 1 November).
notes.tip: Don't present Halloween as an American invention. It comes from the Irish and Celtic Samhain, and only the modern commercial customs came back from the USA.

notes.h: Responses to pressure on everyday culture
notes.b: Communities do not simply accept cultural change. Three responses try to keep traditional expressions alive.
points: Revival movements, such as the Gaelic Revival, promote Irish games and music to keep them in everyday use.
UNESCO's list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity (living traditions and skills rather than buildings or objects) was created by its 2003 convention. Irish harping was added in 2019.
State support for traditional music, sport and arts events helps keep these expressions in practice, because funding lets them continue and reach new audiences.
notes.tip: Exams ask for comment on globalisation. Pair each pressure, such as Americanisation, with a response such as revival, UNESCO listing or State support.

notes.b: Migration (people moving to live in another country) also changes everyday culture, because migrants bring their own customs with them.
points: Migrants bring new food, festivals, religious celebrations and sports, which become part of everyday life in their new country.
New and existing expressions blend: multicultural festivals and fusion food (dishes that mix cooking traditions) combine traditions from different groups.
notes.tip: Exams expect comment on migration as well as globalisation, so include a point on how new customs arrive and blend.

notes.h: Sport: the GAA, its founding and structure
notes.b: The Gaelic Athletic Association (GAA) promotes native Irish games, chiefly hurling and Gaelic football. It is the strongest example of sport as an expression of Irish identity, so be ready to treat it in depth.
points: The GAA was founded on 1 November 1884 in Hayes' Hotel, Thurles, Co. Tipperary, by Michael Cusack and others, to preserve and promote native Irish games.
Maurice Davin was the GAA's first president.
Players are amateurs, so the games stay rooted in the community, which means they play for their club and county without being paid.
Clubs are based on parishes and teams represent counties, so the GAA reinforces local and county identity.
The GAA is organised on an all-island basis and has clubs among the Irish diaspora (Irish people living abroad).
Camogie, the women's form of hurling, is run by the Camogie Association, founded in 1904. Ladies' football is the women's form of Gaelic football.
Hurling was added to UNESCO's list of living traditions in 2018. It is a cultural symbol and is not Ireland's national sport by law.
notes.tip: Don't call hurling Ireland's national sport by law. Say it is a cultural symbol.

notes.h: Sport: Croke Park, rule changes and Bloody Sunday
notes.b: Croke Park is the stadium behind the GAA's best-known rule changes and events, so you can use it to show how sport and national history are linked.
points: Croke Park, Dublin, holds about 82,300 spectators and is one of Europe's largest stadiums.
Members were banned from playing "foreign games" (soccer, rugby, cricket and hockey), which kept the GAA focused on native Irish games. The ban was removed in 1971.
A rule barring members of the British security forces from the GAA was removed in 2001.
Bloody Sunday, 21 November 1920: British forces opened fire at a Gaelic football match in Croke Park, killing 14 people.
This is a different event from Bloody Sunday 1972 in Derry, and there is more on it in the notes on Religion as a cultural indicator.
From 2007 Croke Park hosted rugby and soccer internationals while Lansdowne Road was rebuilt. England played Ireland at rugby there in February 2007.
notes.tip: Keep Bloody Sunday 1920 (Croke Park, 14 killed) separate from Bloody Sunday 1972 (Derry). For rule changes give only the 1971 and 2001 dates.

notes.h: Sport and identity beyond the GAA
notes.b: Other sports express identity too, and in Northern Ireland the team a person supports can signal which community they belong to.
points: The Ireland rugby team represents the whole island, including Northern Ireland, so it is an all-island expression of identity.
Sporting loyalties in Northern Ireland are divided between Irish and British teams, so the choice of team can express national identity.

notes.b: Traditional music is played informally, and sessions are the main setting in which it is shared.
points: Traditional instruments include the fiddle, uilleann pipes (Irish bellows-blown bagpipes), tin whistle, flute, concertina, accordion, bodhrán (a hand-held frame drum) and harp.
The harp is Ireland's national symbol and appears on coins and the presidential seal.
Sessions are informal gatherings where musicians play together, which is how tunes and playing styles are passed on.
Uilleann piping was added to UNESCO's list of living traditions in 2017.
notes.tip: Exams ask about music and dance as a group. Name instruments and sessions, then add Comhaltas, sean-nós and Riverdance.

notes.h: Comhaltas, the Fleadh Cheoil and sean-nós
notes.b: Traditional music has an organisation behind it and a yearly festival, and it has a singing and dancing side too.
points: Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann was founded in 1951 to promote traditional music.
The first Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann (a national music festival) was held in Mullingar in 1951. It is now held in a different town each August and draws hundreds of thousands of visitors.
Sean-nós ("old style") is unaccompanied traditional singing in Irish, strongest in Conamara.
Sean-nós dancing is the traditional informal dance form that sits alongside the singing tradition.

notes.h: Riverdance and the global spread of Irish dance
notes.b: Irish music and dance also reached a world audience, which shows an Irish expression spreading outwards through globalisation.
points: Riverdance began as the interval act (the performance between entries) of the Eurovision Song Contest, performed in Dublin on 30 April 1994.
It became a worldwide touring show, carrying Irish dance to audiences abroad.
Irish popular music with traditional roots combines the traditional instruments and melodies with modern styles.

notes.b: Festivals bring a community together on a fixed date. These points cover national and religious occasions, and St Patrick's Day shows Irish identity in the diaspora.
points: St Patrick's Day, 17 March: parades are held across the world, for example in New York, and landmarks are lit green.
St Patrick's Day is a global expression of Irish identity in the diaspora. Dublin's St Patrick's Festival began in 1996.
St Brigid's Day (Lá Fhéile Bríde, around 1 February) became a public holiday in 2023, the first named after a woman.
Samhain (31 October to 1 November) is the Celtic origin of Halloween.
notes.tip: Present St Patrick's Day as a global expression of Irish identity in the diaspora, and Halloween as having Celtic origins in Samhain.

notes.h: Summer and autumn festivals and fairs
notes.b: Local festivals and fairs tie a place to a custom, and each of these is held at the same time every year.
points: Puck Fair, Killorglin, Co. Kerry, is held every August (10-12 August), when a wild goat is crowned king.
Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival, Co. Clare, is held every September.
Ballinasloe Horse Fair, Co. Galway, is held every October and is one of Europe's oldest horse fairs. It is also important to Travellers, a group with a distinct everyday culture.
notes.tip: Name the place with the festival, and don't add visitor numbers or economic values, which are not checked.

notes.b: Some festivals look outwards to the diaspora, and others celebrate writing and the arts.
points: The Rose of Tralee, Co. Kerry, has been held since 1959 and is open to women of Irish birth or descent worldwide, so it links Ireland with its diaspora.
Bloomsday, 16 June, celebrates James Joyce's Ulysses, which is set on 16 June 1904.
The Galway International Arts Festival has been held since 1978. Wexford Festival Opera has been held since 1951.

notes.b: Some customs go back much further than the modern festivals above.
points: Wakes (gatherings held when someone has died), holy wells and pattern days (feast days held at holy wells) are older Irish traditions that are still practised in some places.

notes.b: What people wear and make can show where they come from. Irish costume and craft range from a handknit jumper to a team jersey.
points: The Aran sweater is a knitted wool jumper from the Aran Islands, Co. Galway.
The Claddagh ring shows two hands holding a heart with a crown. It is named after the Claddagh area of Galway city.
Irish dancing costumes are worn for performances and competitions.
GAA jerseys are everyday dress that shows county identity: supporters wear their county colours.
notes.tip: Exams expect costume and food alongside sport and music. Give each costume item its place.

notes.b: Food is an everyday expression of identity, and several Irish dishes are tied to particular places.
points: Traditional dishes include soda bread, Irish stew, colcannon, boxty, coddle and the full Irish breakfast.
Boxty is a potato pancake associated with the north midlands and Connacht.
Coddle is a Dublin dish, so some Irish foods are tied to a particular place.
Guinness has been brewed at St James's Gate, Dublin, since 1759, so it is a long-standing Irish drink.

notes.h: Food and change through migration and globalisation
notes.b: Irish food is not fixed. Immigration has added new foods to the traditional ones.
points: Census 2022 recorded Polish as the most common home language after English and Irish.
Polish shops and Polish food are now common in Irish towns, so new foods sit beside traditional dishes.

notes.h: Early Christian art and ancient monuments
notes.b: Irish art and monuments from the distant past are still expressions of identity today.
points: The Book of Kells is an illuminated gospel manuscript (a hand-written book of the gospels with decorated pages) made around 800. It is kept at Trinity College Dublin.
High crosses, such as Muiredach's Cross at Monasterboice, Co. Louth, are carved stone monuments of early Christian Ireland.
Newgrange (Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath) is a passage tomb (a burial mound with a long entrance passage) built around 3200 BC and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Sunlight enters the chamber at Newgrange at the winter solstice (the shortest day of the year).

notes.b: Writing is another way in which Irish identity is expressed, in English and in Irish.
points: Irish Nobel Prize winners for Literature are W. B. Yeats (1923), George Bernard Shaw (1925), Samuel Beckett (1969) and Seamus Heaney (1995).
Irish-language literature and songs express identity through the language itself. There is more on this in the notes on Language as a cultural indicator.

notes.b: Irish Travellers are a group with a distinct everyday culture of their own.
points: Irish Travellers have a distinct everyday culture, traditionally nomadic (moving from place to place) and based on strong extended family ties.
Horse fairs are important to Travellers, for example the Ballinasloe Horse Fair in Co. Galway.
Travellers have their own language, known as Cant, Gammon or Shelta.
There is more on their recognition as an ethnic minority in the notes on Racial groupings.

notes.h: Parades, murals and territorial markers in Northern Ireland
notes.b: In Northern Ireland, parades and painted symbols express two opposing identities: unionist (wanting to remain in the United Kingdom) and nationalist (wanting a united Ireland). Here you need only the expressions, not the conflict.
points: Orange Order parades on 12 July commemorate the Battle of the Boyne (1690). Bonfires are lit on the night of 11 July in loyalist areas (areas of strong unionist, pro-British identity).
Parades express unionist identity and can divide communities. There is more on the conflict itself in the notes on Religion as a cultural indicator.
Painted gable-end murals (pictures on the end walls of houses) in Belfast and Derry show loyalist and republican identities.
Kerbstones are painted red, white and blue or green, white and orange to mark territory.

notes.b: Spain is the first European example. Its festivals range from religious processions to a tomato fight, and some express regional identity.
points: San Fermín in Pamplona, Navarre, runs from 6 to 14 July and includes the running of the bulls through the streets.
La Tomatina in Buñol, near Valencia, is a tomato fight held on the last Wednesday of August. It has been held since 1945.
Semana Santa (Holy Week, the week before Easter) features religious processions, especially in Seville.
Flamenco, the song, guitar and dance of Andalusia, has been on UNESCO's list since 2010.
Castells, human towers built in Catalonia, have been on UNESCO's list since 2010 and express Catalan regional identity.

notes.b: Football, bullfighting and food in Spain show how regional identities are expressed, and sometimes contested.
points: FC Barcelona's motto, "Més que un club" ("More than a club"), reflects its role as a symbol of Catalan identity, especially under Franco (Spain's dictator, who suppressed regional identities).
Athletic Bilbao fields only players born or raised in the Basque Country, or trained in Basque clubs, which makes the team an expression of Basque identity.
Catalonia's parliament banned bullfighting in 2010, with the ban in force from 2012. Spain's Constitutional Court overturned the ban in 2016.
Paella comes from Valencia. Tapas are small dishes shared in bars.

notes.b: Scotland offers a second example, with distinctive dress, music and festivals.
points: The kilt, worn with tartan (a woven pattern of crossing coloured stripes), is the best-known Scottish dress.
Bagpipes are played by pipe bands and at Highland Games.
Highland Games are traditional sports such as the caber toss (throwing a long wooden pole) and hammer throw, held with piping and Highland dancing.
Burns Night, 25 January, celebrates the poet Robert Burns with haggis, whisky and poetry.
Hogmanay is the Scottish New Year celebration, so Scotland marks the new year in its own way.
notes.tip: Don't claim that Scottish clan tartans date from ancient times. That is not checked.

notes.b: In Glasgow two football clubs carry religious and national identities, which is why their rivalry is more than a sporting one.
points: Celtic FC was founded in 1887 in Glasgow's East End by Brother Walfrid, a Marist brother (a member of a Catholic religious order), to raise money for poor Irish Catholic immigrants.
Rangers was founded in 1872 and was traditionally supported by Protestants and unionists.
The rivalry between the two clubs, known as the Old Firm, carries religious and Irish or British identity.

notes.b: Germany's examples combine a long-running festival, regional dress and food shaped by migration.
points: Oktoberfest in Munich, Bavaria, has been held since 1810. It began with a royal wedding.
Visitors to Oktoberfest wear lederhosen (Bavarian leather shorts) and dirndl (a traditional Bavarian dress).
Christmas markets are held in German cities.
The döner kebab became popular in Germany through Turkish immigrants, an example of migration adding to everyday food.

notes.h: France: national day, sport and film
notes.b: France's examples include a national day, a cycle race, food and a film festival.
points: Bastille Day, 14 July, commemorates the storming of the Bastille in 1789 and is marked by a military parade in Paris.
The Tour de France cycle race was first held in 1903 and takes place each July.
The "gastronomic meal of the French" was added to UNESCO's list in 2010.
The Cannes Film Festival is held each May, which makes film one of France's expressions of culture.

notes.b: French public life is shaped by a principle of keeping religion and the state apart.
points: Laïcité, the principle of state secularism (keeping religion out of government and public institutions), shapes the debate over religious dress in public life. There is more on this in the notes on Religion as a cultural indicator.

notes.b: Italy's expressions are strongly tied to local districts and regions.
points: The Palio di Siena is a horse race around the Piazza del Campo between the city's districts, the contrade, held on 2 July and 16 August.
Venice Carnival, with its masks, takes place before Lent (the period of fasting before Easter).
Neapolitan pizza-making was added to UNESCO's list in 2017.
Regional food is central to Italian identity, with pizza from Naples and pasta as the main examples.
Football is also a major Italian sporting expression, for example alongside the Palio.

notes.b: These shorter examples can be used when you need extra European material, one point each.
points: Norway's Constitution Day, 17 May, marks the constitution of 1814 with children's parades and the bunad, a regional folk costume.
King's Day in the Netherlands, 27 April, sees people dress in orange, the colour of the royal House of Orange.
The Festival Interceltique de Lorient in Brittany has been held every August since 1971 and brings together musicians from the Celtic regions.
Fest-noz, the Breton night dance festival, has been on UNESCO's list since 2012.
The National Eisteddfod of Wales is an annual festival of Welsh music, poetry and culture held entirely in Welsh.
There is more on festivals in Switzerland and the Balkans in the notes on A European regional case study of identity.

notes.h: Eurovision as a European cultural event
notes.b: Eurovision is a European-wide event, and Ireland has a strong record in it.
points: The Eurovision Song Contest is a European-wide event in which countries present national acts, so it also expresses national identity and politics.
Ireland has won the contest seven times, including three in a row in 1992-94.
notes.tip: Give only Ireland's seven wins and the 1992-94 run. Don't claim Ireland holds the record outright, because Sweden has also won seven times.

keyTerms.definition: A visible, practised part of culture, such as a sport, custom, dish or festival, that people choose, repeat and pass on.
The body founded in 1884 to promote native Irish games, organised by parish clubs and county teams.
A movement that promoted Irish games, music and culture to assert Irish identity under pressure.
Unaccompanied traditional singing in Irish, meaning “old style”, strongest in Conamara.
The annual traditional music festival organised by Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, held in a different town each August.
The Celtic festival from 31 October to 1 November, the origin of Halloween.
Human towers built by teams in Catalonia, placed on UNESCO’s list in 2010.
A regional folk costume worn in Norway, including on Constitution Day.
The French principle of state secularism, which shapes debate over religious dress in public life.
A people living outside their homeland who keep their cultural identity, for example through St Patrick’s Day parades.

factCards.term: Everyday expressions of culture: five reasons they matter
factCards.definition: They mark belonging; they pass culture between generations; they assert identity under pressure, as Irish games and music did in the Gaelic Revival; they attract tourists and income; they can mark division (Northern Ireland parades, football rivalries).

factCards.term: Globalisation and everyday culture: pressures and responses
factCards.definition: Fast food, Hollywood, global sports and brands make cultures alike: McDonald's opened on Grafton Street in 1977; Halloween customs returned from the USA in commercial form. Responses: revival movements, State support, UNESCO's intangible heritage list.

factCards.term: Name three Irish entries on UNESCO's intangible heritage list, with years
factCards.definition: Uilleann piping (2017), hurling (2018) and Irish harping (2019), recorded as living traditions under UNESCO's 2003 convention on the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

factCards.term: Migration and everyday culture: effects with two examples
factCards.definition: Migrants bring food, festivals, religious celebrations and sports that blend with local ones in multicultural festivals and fusion food: Polish shops and food are now common in Irish towns; the döner kebab spread in Germany through Turkish immigrants.

factCards.term: The GAA: founding, aims and structure
factCards.definition: Founded 1 November 1884 at Hayes' Hotel, Thurles, by Michael Cusack and others (first president Maurice Davin) to preserve native games. Amateur; parish clubs and county teams build local identity; all-island, with diaspora clubs; Camogie Association, 1904.

factCards.term: Croke Park: capacity, Bloody Sunday 1920 and the 2007 opening
factCards.definition: Holds about 82,300, one of Europe's largest stadiums. 21 November 1920: British forces fired on a Gaelic football match, killing 14. From 2007 it hosted rugby and soccer while Lansdowne Road was rebuilt; England played Ireland at rugby there in February 2007.

factCards.term: GAA rule changes and sporting identity beyond the GAA
factCards.definition: The ban on foreign games (soccer, rugby, cricket, hockey) was lifted in 1971; the rule barring British security forces in 2001. The Ireland rugby team represents the whole island; in Northern Ireland, backing Irish or British teams can express identity.

factCards.term: Irish traditional music: instruments, organisations and the Fleadh
factCards.definition: Fiddle, uilleann pipes, tin whistle, flute, concertina, accordion, bodhrán and harp (the national symbol). Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann, 1951; first Fleadh Cheoil, Mullingar, 1951, now in a different town each August. Sean-nós singing is strongest in Conamara.

factCards.term: Riverdance and Eurovision: Ireland on the European stage
factCards.definition: Riverdance began as the interval act of the Eurovision Song Contest in Dublin on 30 April 1994 and became a worldwide touring show, spreading Irish dance. Ireland has won Eurovision seven times, including three in a row, 1992–94.

factCards.term: Irish national festivals: St Patrick's Day, St Brigid's Day and Samhain
factCards.definition: St Patrick's Day, 17 March: parades worldwide (e.g. New York), landmarks lit green, Dublin festival since 1996. St Brigid's Day (around 1 February): public holiday from 2023, the first named after a woman. Samhain (31 October–1 November): origin of Halloween.

factCards.term: Irish fairs and older traditions: places and timing
factCards.definition: Puck Fair, Killorglin, Co. Kerry, 10–12 August, when a wild goat is crowned king; Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival, Co. Clare, each September; Ballinasloe Horse Fair, each October, one of Europe's oldest. Older traditions: wakes, holy wells, pattern days.

factCards.term: Irish diaspora, literary and arts festivals with dates
factCards.definition: Rose of Tralee, since 1959, open to women of Irish birth or descent worldwide; Bloomsday, 16 June, for Joyce's Ulysses (set on 16 June 1904); Galway International Arts Festival, since 1978; Wexford Festival Opera, since 1951.

factCards.term: Irish costume, craft and food as expressions of identity
factCards.definition: Aran sweater from the Aran Islands; Claddagh ring (hands, heart, crown) from Galway's Claddagh; dancing costumes; county GAA jerseys. Food: soda bread, Irish stew, colcannon, boxty, Dublin coddle, full Irish breakfast; Guinness at St James's Gate since 1759.

factCards.term: Irish art and literature: Newgrange, early Christian art and Nobel laureates
factCards.definition: Book of Kells (around 800, Trinity College Dublin); high crosses such as Muiredach's Cross, Monasterboice; Newgrange (around 3200 BC), lit at the winter solstice. Nobel Prize for Literature: Yeats 1923, Shaw 1925, Beckett 1969, Heaney 1995.

factCards.term: Irish Travellers: features of their everyday culture
factCards.definition: Traditionally nomadic, with strong extended family ties; horse fairs such as Ballinasloe; their own language, Cant, Gammon or Shelta; about 33,000 people (Census 2022), recognised as an ethnic minority on 1 March 2017.

factCards.term: Northern Ireland: parades, murals and territorial markers
factCards.definition: Orange Order parades on 12 July mark the Battle of the Boyne (1690), with loyalist bonfires on 11 July; murals in Belfast and Derry show loyalist and republican identities; kerbstones painted red, white and blue or green, white and orange mark territory.

factCards.term: Spain: festivals with places and dates
factCards.definition: San Fermín, Pamplona, 6–14 July, with the running of the bulls; La Tomatina, Buñol, last Wednesday of August, since 1945; Semana Santa processions, especially in Seville; flamenco (Andalusia) and Catalan castells, both on UNESCO's list since 2010.

factCards.term: Spain: football, bullfighting and regional identity
factCards.definition: FC Barcelona's motto Més que un club reflects its role as a symbol of Catalan identity, especially under Franco; Athletic Bilbao fields only players born, raised or trained in the Basque Country; Catalonia banned bullfighting in 2010 (in force 2012), overturned in 2016.

factCards.term: Scotland: dress, music and festivals
factCards.definition: Kilt and tartan; bagpipes; Highland Games (caber toss, hammer throw, piping, Highland dancing); Burns Night, 25 January, celebrating Robert Burns with haggis, whisky and poetry; Hogmanay, the Scottish New Year.

factCards.term: Celtic and Rangers: football as religious and national identity
factCards.definition: Celtic was founded in 1887 in Glasgow's East End by Brother Walfrid to raise money for poor Irish Catholic immigrants; Rangers (1872) was traditionally backed by Protestants and unionists. The Old Firm rivalry carries religious and Irish or British identity.

factCards.term: Germany: everyday expressions of culture with dates
factCards.definition: Oktoberfest, Munich, Bavaria, held since 1810, when it began with a royal wedding; visitors wear lederhosen and dirndl; Christmas markets in German cities; the döner kebab, popularised by Turkish immigrants, shows migration changing everyday food.

factCards.term: France: everyday expressions of culture with dates
factCards.definition: Bastille Day, 14 July, marks the storming of the Bastille (1789) with a military parade in Paris; the Tour de France, first held 1903, each July; the gastronomic meal of the French, on UNESCO's list since 2010; the Cannes Film Festival each May.

factCards.term: Italy: festivals and food as expressions of identity
factCards.definition: Palio di Siena: a horse race around the Piazza del Campo between the city's contrade, on 2 July and 16 August; Venice Carnival, with masks, before Lent; Neapolitan pizza-making on UNESCO's list since 2017; regional food and football.

factCards.term: Norway, the Netherlands and Brittany: national and regional festivals
factCards.definition: Norway: Constitution Day, 17 May (1814 constitution), with children's parades and the bunad. Netherlands: King's Day, 27 April, when people wear orange. Brittany: Festival Interceltique de Lorient each August since 1971; fest-noz on UNESCO's list since 2012.

questions.prompt: Examine how people express their culture and identity in everyday life, with reference to Irish examples.
questions.model: Four aspects. Sport: the GAA in depth, covering its founding in 1884, its parish and county structure, Bloody Sunday in 1920 and the 1971 and 2001 rule changes, with hurling on UNESCO’s list. Music and dance: traditional instruments, sessions, Comhaltas and the Fleadh Cheoil, sean-nós and Riverdance. Festivals and traditions: St Patrick’s Day, St Brigid’s Day, Samhain, Puck Fair, Lisdoonvarna, the Rose of Tralee and Bloomsday. Costume, food and art: the Aran sweater, the Claddagh ring and GAA jerseys; soda bread, Irish stew and Guinness; the Book of Kells, Newgrange and the Irish Nobel laureates. Close with one point on globalisation, such as McDonald’s opening in Dublin in 1977, or on the culture of the Travellers. Irish examples only. About 25 to 30 significant relevant points.

questions.prompt: Examine how people express their culture and identity in everyday life, with reference to European examples.
questions.model: Spain: festivals (San Fermín, La Tomatina, Semana Santa), flamenco, the castells and regional identity, and football (FC Barcelona and Catalonia; Athletic Bilbao’s Basque-only policy). Scotland: dress and the kilt, bagpipes and Highland Games, Burns Night and Hogmanay, and the Old Firm of Celtic and Rangers. Germany or France as a third example: Oktoberfest and the dirndl and lederhosen, or Bastille Day, the Tour de France and the gastronomic meal of the French. One point on globalisation, such as the spread of döner kebab through Turkish immigration or the spread of fast food. About 25 to 30 significant relevant points.

questions.prompt: Explain how sport can express cultural identity, with reference to examples.
questions.model: The GAA: its founding in 1884 to preserve native games, its parish and county structure that reinforces local and county identity, the Bloody Sunday shooting at Croke Park in 1920, and the 1971 and 2001 rule changes that ended the bans. FC Barcelona as a symbol of Catalan identity, and Athletic Bilbao’s Basque-only player policy. Celtic and Rangers as expressions of religious and Irish or British identity.
